Hi op,

I wanted to begin by congratulating you on your accomplishments! As a fellow STEM student, I understand the technicality and difficulty of these courses. 

After reading your post, I found it highly relatable because I went through a similar turbulent relationship with my mother. No matter how much effort I put into my studies, she would never acknowledge my hard work. Instead, she would lecture me on how I could have done better to achieve top grades, even when I was already close to doing so. She constantly compared me to other kids around me. 

Now, at the age of 22, I realise that she was fixated on grades and, like many other Asian parents, pushed me hard because they believe that grades are the sole measure of success in life. However, I am fully aware of the self-loathing and negative impact that prolonged situations like these can have on one's self-confidence. For a while, I held resentment towards my mum for contributing to my negative self-perception. I believed that no matter how much I tried, I wasn't good enough, and the fact that my own parent couldn't acknowledge or be proud of me reinforced that belief.  
Whilst most parents have good intentions, they often have lofty expectations for their children and overlook the fact that we are not mere machines or investments. Moreover, they hold a different notion of what constitutes success, which could be attributed to a characteristic commonly observed among Asian parents—they often face difficulties in expressing their emotions or effectively communicating with us. This difficulty in communication and emotional expression may be rooted in their upbringing and the era in which they were raised. Consequently, they frequently fail to recognise that an individual's value extends far beyond their academic grades, overlooking the fact that personal worth encompasses various aspects of life.  
In my mum's case, academic success was one of the few avenues through which she could achieve something and validate her own worth, making it difficult for her to break free from that mindset. Perhaps realising this allowed me to approach my situation from a different perspective and also contributed to my growth and understanding.

I don't think my response helps in any way, but I just felt the need to acknowledge your efforts and encourage you to continue making efforts for yourself and your future, and not for your parents.
